title: Exocytosis in Cellular Physiology
subject: Physiology
summary: Exocytosis moves substances from inside the cell to the extracellular space using vesicle fusion. It underpins neurotransmission, hormone release, and digestive enzyme secretion, and its failure causes several clinical syndromes.

sections.p: Exocytosis is the process by which cells export cargo—neurotransmitters, hormones, enzymes—via membrane‑bound vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane.
b: Key for synaptic transmission, endocrine signaling, and pancreatic secretion
Requires calcium influx and SNARE protein complex

sections.p: An action potential opens voltage‑gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ binds synaptotagmin, triggering SNARE proteins (syntaxin, SNAP‑25, VAMP) to pull vesicle and plasma membranes together, forming a fusion pore.
b: Fusion pore expands, cargo released, vesicle membrane becomes part of plasma membrane

sections.p: Calcium concentration is the primary trigger; accessory proteins (Munc13, complexin) modulate speed and fidelity. Hormonal signals (e.g., cAMP) can prime vesicles for rapid release.
b: Low intracellular Ca²⁺ → vesicles remain docked but inactive
Second‑messenger pathways can increase vesicle pool size

sections.p: Defective exocytosis leads to impaired neurotransmission, endocrine failure, or pancreatic autodigestion.
b: Botulism toxin cleaves SNAP‑25 → paralytic weakness
Familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (defective perforin exocytosis) → severe immune dysregulation
Acute pancreatitis from blocked zymogen granule exocytosis → intracellular activation of enzymes

sections.p: Understanding exocytosis guides diagnosis and treatment of neurotoxic poisoning, endocrine emergencies, and pancreatic disease, especially where advanced imaging is unavailable.
b: Identify botulism by descending flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes
Recognise acute pancreatitis by epigastric pain, raised amylase/lipase, and lack of gallstone imaging
Interpret insulinoma suspicion when hypoglycaemia persists despite fasting

t.b: Confirms pancreatic enzyme leakage; >3× upper limit supports acute pancreatitis
Detects toxin; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture and epidemiology
Demonstrates Whipple's triad for insulinoma; if glucometer unavailable, use bedside capillary glucose

sections.p: Focus on mechanism‑clinical links, bedside clues, and management priorities when resources are limited.
b: Link calcium‑triggered exocytosis to the rapid onset of neuromuscular symptoms in botulism
Explain why secretin test is rarely used in low‑resource settings for pancreatic assessment

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive respiratory muscle weakness in suspected botulism
Severe epigastric pain with vomiting and hypotension suggesting necrotising pancreatitis
Recurrent hypoglycaemia causing seizures or loss of consciousness

faq.q: Why does botulism cause flaccid paralysis?
faq.a: The toxin cleaves SNAP‑25, preventing vesicle fusion and acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction.

faq.q: How can you differentiate pancreatitis from other causes of abdominal pain without imaging?
faq.a: Rely on characteristic pain radiating to the back, vomiting, and serum amylase/lipase >3× normal.

faq.q: What bedside test indicates impaired exocytosis of insulin?
faq.a: A supervised fast showing plasma glucose <55 mg/dL with inappropriately high insulin (>5 µU/mL).

exam: A patient presents with descending weakness after eating home‑preserved fish; what toxin mechanism explains the findings — inhibition of SNARE‑mediated exocytosis of acetylcholine.
In a febrile child with sudden onset of flaccid paralysis, which bedside sign confirms a presynaptic problem — absent deep tendon reflexes with preserved sensation.
You suspect acute pancreatitis but ultrasound is unavailable; which laboratory result is most diagnostic and why — amylase or lipase >3× upper limit indicates pancreatic enzyme leakage.
Explain why giving anticholinesterase drugs in botulism can be harmful — they increase acetylcholine but the release machinery is blocked, providing little benefit and risk of cholinergic excess.

A patient with HIV develops severe abdominal pain and elevated lipase; what extra cause should you consider and how does it relate to exocytosis — opportunistic CMV pancreatitis causing duct obstruction and impaired enzyme secretion.

During a malaria outbreak, a child develops hypoglycaemia unresponsive to glucose; which endocrine exocytosis defect should you suspect — impaired glucagon release due to parasite‑induced β‑cell dysfunction.
Describe the first emergency step for a patient with suspected botulism — secure airway and provide mechanical ventilation if respiratory muscles are compromised.
Why is secretin stimulation test rarely used in low‑resource hospitals for pancreatic disease — it requires intravenous secretin and serial enzyme measurements unavailable in most settings.
